items.title: New TypoPrompting Attacks Turn Mistyped AI Website Addresses Into Malware Installation Traps
items.summary: A simple typing mistake can now cost you more than a failed page load. Researchers have found that mistyped addresses of popular AI tools lead to fake verification pages, hidden commands and malware installers. The technique is called TypoPrompting. The research traced 186 lookalike domains across 27 AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs and Cursor. A small slip, such as “cloude.ai” for Claude, can send a visitor down a chain of redirects that ends in a ClickFix lure, a Microsoft Store-signed hijacker or a search-changing browser extension. This follows other reports of fake AI brand lures used to push harmful files and commands. Analysts at Island identified the campaign and named the pattern TypoPrompting. They describe it as AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else. The research was published on November 12, 2026, by lead security researcher Oleg Zaytsev. New TypoPrompting Attacks Turn Mistyped AI Website Addresses The typos are ordinary. In “clsude.ai” the finger hits S instead of A. In “cluade.ai” two letters swap places. In “caude.ai” a letter goes missing. ChatGPT has the most lookalikes at 25, followed by Claude with 18 and DeepSeek with 16. What happens next depends on the visitor. A parked page hands the browser to a traffic distribution system. That system picks a destination based on the visitor’s location, operating system and browser. One person sees a harmless parked page, while another gets a malicious lure. Some of these names are years old. Several were registered in July 2023 and later joined a monetized portfolio of 81 domains tied to the redirector a11[.]click. Three traced AI lookalikes lead to a ClickFix lure (Source – Island) The Claude typo “cloude.ai” shows the full chain. A Windows visitor is sent through several redirect hops to a gate that fingerprints the browser and solves a small proof-of-work challenge. Only selected visits get an answer. That answer is a fake human check, and fake Cloudflare verification pages have been seen in other ClickFix campaigns too. The page tells the user to open the Windows Run box, paste a command and press Enter. The pasted command uses curl to save a script named W901.ps1 in the temporary folder. It then runs the script in a hidden PowerShell window with the execution policy bypassed. The download address is written as the single number 3112851459. This is the IP address 185.138.88[.]3 in decimal form, so a filter looking for dotted IP addresses would miss it. The gate behind this chain is much larger than one typo. Researchers found 550 matching scan records across 211 entry domains. These include lookalikes of Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Verizon and Microsoft Azure. Mac users get a fake Terminal prompt instead, and others are offered an archive to unpack and run. Store-Signed Malware and Search Hijacking A second route ends somewhere that looks far safer. Eight typos of Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs and Voice AI led through deezyj[.]com to fake “Security Check” pages. These pages delivered Net Guard, an app sold as a Wi-Fi and DNS scanner. The installer matches the real Microsoft Store listing and carries Microsoft’s signature, so victims get a genuine Store package with a browser-control engine inside. Net Guard is built on a module called buntai-sdk and takes its orders from remote configuration. It can change the default search engine while the user is idle. It can also run remote JavaScript through browser DevTools and edit browser profiles to install extensions. In the code the researchers analyzed, all of these features are on by default. The app also checks for a debugger and for enterprise browser management. Privacy Keeper and MyFlixly Browser share the same code and were also classed as malicious browser hijackers. The Net Guard chain (Source – Island) The third route starts at “preplexity.ai”, a Perplexity typo. It leads to an installation page for a Chrome extension that needs no permissions. Its listing promises Bing search, but its manifest quietly sends every address-bar search through find.flashysearches[.]com. It is one of 30 extensions built from one kit. Thirteen have been removed, and the 17 still listed showed 972,000 users on November 3. This matches the pattern in a recent report on Chrome extensions hijacking searches at a much larger scale. Island advises organizations to give staff direct links to approved AI services and to watch for lookalikes of those tools. It also suggests linking browsing activity to Run-dialog or Terminal use, checking the publisher and hash of MSIX installers, and setting a fixed search provider. Security teams should hunt across the whole route, from entry domain to endpoint change. The same human-error risk appears when slopsquatting targets AI coding agents , where a wrong name leads to malware. Users can lower the risk by bookmarking the AI tools they use. A real verification page never asks you to paste a command. Key Takeaways
  • At 1,252 CVEs this month, “patch everything now” isn’t a plan; teams need to decide what to patch first, what to test, and what to mitigate.
  • Know your exposure early: Qualys InstaScan flagged affected assets about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s release notes page finished loading, with no new scan.
  • Not every patch is safe on day one: about 35% of November patches earned a Low reliability rating from Qualys, based on public signals and telemetry from 500M+ deployed patches.
  • Deploy in waves: proven risky exposures first, low-impact patches on automation, and high-impact patches through pilot rings.
  • When a critical patch breaks, mitigate with a compensating control, then patch and retire the mitigation once a fixed update ships.

Every Patch Tuesday forces the same trade-off. Patch too slowly, and attackers get a head start on newly disclosed vulnerabilities. Patch too quickly, and a bad update can take down Exchange, break line-of-business apps, or trigger a wave of help desk tickets.

November 2026 showed both sides of that tension. Our data pointed to three lessons security and IT teams can use this month and every month:

  • Know your exposure before the details are public
  • Check whether a patch is reliable before you push it
  • Have a fallback when it isn’t
November at a glance

In November 2025, Microsoft addressed 63 CVEs on Patch Tuesday. In November 2026, with frontier AI models now accelerating vulnerability discovery, that number reached 1,252, nearly 20 times higher. And this isn’t an isolated month. Since April 2026, Microsoft has addressed an average of roughly 650 CVEs per month, nearly nine times the average of about 74 between November 2025 and March 2026. Each of the last three releases has addressed close to 1,000 CVEs or more.

With the same size team, manual patching can’t keep up. No team’s manual patching capacity has grown twentyfold in a year, and that gap is why speed alone isn’t enough.

The vulnerabilities worth knowing about:

  • Outlook NTLMv2 hash disclosure (CVE-2026-124194). This one is exploited in the wild despite a Moderate rating. Opening a crafted message file skips Outlook’s external-content warning and leaks the user’s NTLMv2 hash to an attacker-controlled server.
  • Exchange Server remote code execution (CVE-2026-118207). Rated Critical. An authenticated attacker with low-level access can run code on on-premises Exchange, and Microsoft rates exploitation more likely. If you run Exchange on Windows Server 2019, November hands you both problems at once: a critical Exchange flaw to close, and an OS update reported to break Exchange.
  • Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution (CVE-2026-118146). A crafted request from a low-privileged user could run code on domain controllers. Exploitation is rated more likely.
  • Recurring pressure points. Office and Outlook Preview Pane RCEs are back for a third month in a row, alongside a new zero-click Windows Search RCE and more Hyper-V escapes.

At this volume, “patch everything now” isn’t a plan. The real questions are what to patch first, what to test, and what to do when a patch can’t go out.

The three insights below answer those questions in the order they come up during a Patch Tuesday cycle: knowing your exposure as updates land, checking whether a patch is safe to deploy, and falling back to mitigation when it isn’t.

Insight 1:  The faster you know your exposure, the sooner you can act

On November 10, Qualys InstaScan picked up Microsoft’s November security updates from Microsoft’s API the moment they were released. It began evaluating customer assets right away, roughly 40 minutes before Microsoft’s public release notes page finished loading. During that window, the page still showed a “{{release}}” placeholder in its title.

By the time most teams were reading the bulletin, InstaScan users already had a list of affected assets in front of them: more than 11,000 Microsoft findings in the InstaScan view, each marked “first found a few seconds ago.”

Why it matters: the first hours after Patch Tuesday are when prioritization happens, and attackers are using AI to create exploits after a patch is released faster than ever. Teams that know which assets are exposed before the details go public can plan rings, line up change windows, and flag critical systems sooner, instead of starting from a blank spreadsheet.

Note: InstaScan, powered by Qualys Agent Insta, works from the inventory and telemetry Qualys already collects, so no new scan is needed.

Insight 2: Not every patch is ready on day one

As of 3 p.m. MT on November 11, about 35% of this month’s patches carried a Low reliability rating in Qualys’s AI-powered Patch Reliability Assessment. The rating combines public signals on every patch, such as vendor KBs and advisories, Linux release notes and sysadmin forums, with Qualys telemetry from more than 500 million deployed patches, including real rollback and vulnerability-reopen rates.Low reliability doesn’t mean “don’t patch.” It means “don’t patch blind.”

Example: KB5131085. Microsoft rated this cumulative update for Windows 10 / Windows Server 2019 (OS Build 17763.9487) Critical. It addresses CVE-2026-119892 and 574 other CVEs. It also earned a Low reliability rating, with two issues reported by the community:

  • Exchange Server deployments may see sign-in, mailbox access and mail queue failures.
  • USB Audio Class 1.0 devices may fail to start or lose audio output (Code 10).

For a team running Exchange on Server 2019, that’s the difference between a routine update and a messaging outage.

And it’s not an isolated case. Recent vendor-confirmed examples include a November SQL Server update (KB5129299) that can cause access violations when querying sys.dm_exec_requests during recovery, with no fix yet and a trace-flag workaround, and an October .NET Framework update for Windows 11 (KB5127694) that fails to install with error 0x800F0922 and rolls back after reboot.

No team’s manual patching capacity has grown twentyfold in a year. That gap is why speed alone isn’t enough.

What to do: deploy in waves with Agent Sara

Community signals tell you where to look; your own environment tells you whether a patch is safe. The answer isn’t one big push or one long wait. It’s sequencing.

In Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, Agent Sara builds intelligent remediation waves for you. It sorts every fix by risk, operational impact and patch reliability, then routes it to the right rollout: zero-touch first, rings for riskier patches, and patchless fixes where no patch fits.

  • Wave 0: Proven risky exposures. Vulnerabilities on CISA’s KEV list, publicly exposed assets, and flaws an adversary can automate to take total control. These get fixed first.
  • Wave 1: Low operational impact. High-reliability patches for browsers, standalone utilities and non-critical assets that don’t need a reboot. These go out with zero-touch automation.
  • Wave 2: High operational impact. High-reliability patches for shared runtimes, dependencies and critical assets, where reboots are expected. These go out in rings: a small, representative pilot group first, including the configurations most likely to break (for KB5131085, your Exchange servers), then broader rings once the patch holds up.
  • Wave 3: Beyond patching. Low-reliability patches, vulnerabilities with no patch available, and end-of-life apps. These get a mitigation instead (more on that below).
  • Wave 4: Uninstall. Bloatware, unused user-space apps and residual files. Removing them shrinks the attack surface for good.

The result: the riskiest exposures close first, routine patches stop needing hands-on attention, and your team spends its time on the updates that actually need judgment.

Community signals tell you where to look; your own rings tell you whether it applies to you. In Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, Agent Sara builds these remediation waves for you.

Insight 3: When a critical patch breaks, mitigate

Sometimes the pilot ring confirms the bad news: the patch breaks something you can’t live without, yet the vulnerabilities it fixes are critical. Rolling back and waiting for a fix leaves the door open. Pushing it anyway takes the business down.

There’s a third path: mitigate. Apply a compensating control that closes the attack path without installing the update, such as disabling a vulnerable service or feature, changing a registry or configuration setting, or isolating the exposed asset. Keep it in place until the vendor releases a fixed update, then patch and retire the mitigation.

In the news this week: KB5132061. Microsoft has confirmed that its November 2026 security update for Windows 11 (KB5132061) fails to install on some devices that installed the October 2026 non-security preview update (KB5127936). Affected devices may retry the installation repeatedly or return errors 0x80070306, 0x800f0989 or 0x800f0993. Microsoft says the issue will resolve automatically within 24 to 48 hours of November 11, and asks admins to contact support if it persists.

Until then, those devices are missing every fix in this month’s Windows release, and retrying won’t change that. Instead of waiting, teams can identify which devices have KB5127936 installed, apply mitigations for the most critical exposures first, such as anything on CISA’s KEV list or rated exploitation more likely, and let the November update install once Microsoft’s repair lands. Then they retire the mitigations.

The same approach works when there’s no patch at all, or when the software is end-of-life. And for bloatware and unused apps, the cleanest fix is often to uninstall them and shrink the attack surface for good.

With Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, teams can deploy those mitigations at scale from the same platform that detected the exposure, and track which assets are protected by a patch, a mitigation, or neither.

The Patch Tuesday playbook

Speed and stability aren’t opposites if each step has a clear job:

  1. Detect early. Know which assets are exposed as soon as updates are released, not when the bulletin finishes loading.
  2. Assess reliability. Check community signals before deployment so known breakages don’t surprise you.
  3. Deploy in waves. Let Agent Sara sequence the rollout: riskiest exposures first, zero-touch for low-impact patches, rings for critical systems.
  4. Mitigate when the patch breaks. If a critical patch fails in testing, close the risk with a compensating control until a fixed update is available.
Frequently Asked Questions How should security teams prioritize patches after Patch Tuesday?

Deploy in waves. Fix proven risky exposures first, such as vulnerabilities on CISA’s KEV list and publicly exposed assets. Automate high-reliability, low-impact patches, and send high-impact patches through pilot rings.

Is it safe to deploy Patch Tuesday updates on day one?

Not always. In November 2026, about 35% of patches carried a Low reliability rating, including KB5131085, which is reported to break Exchange on Windows Server 2019. A Low rating means test first, not skip the patch.

What is a patch reliability rating?

 It’s an AI-driven rating from Qualys that predicts how likely a patch is to break something in your environment before you deploy it. High reliability means deploy with confidence; Low means test, stage or delay broad rollout.

What is ring-based patch deployment?

It rolls an update out in stages, starting with a small pilot group that includes the configurations most likely to break. Once the patch holds up in your environment, it expands to broader rings.

How do I reduce risk when no patch is available or software is end-of-life?

Use a compensating control to close the attack path. For bloatware and unused apps, the cleanest fix is often to uninstall them and shrink the attack surface for good.

How can I see which assets are affected before Microsoft’s release notes are published?

Qualys InstaScan evaluates assets the moment Microsoft releases updates, with no new scan. In November 2026, it flagged affected assets about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s release notes page finished loading.

items.summary: Hackers are hiding cryptocurrency mining on Linux GPU servers by changing the readings administrators use to spot heavy workloads. The toolkit combines a Rust-based controller called SANSAR, a kernel rootkit, and a modified NVIDIA monitoring library that reports 0% GPU utilization while mining continues in the background. The intrusion reached three Linux GPU hosts through an exposed Ray job agent. Ray supports distributed computing, including AI training and inference, making these systems valuable targets. Unlike campaigns involving fake utility download traps , this attack entered through infrastructure that accepted remote computing jobs without authentication. Researchers from Elastic Security Labs identified the activity as REF3364 in a November 12, 2026, technical analysis of SANSAR. Their findings describe coordinated tools for mining, hiding processes, maintaining access, and opening remote shells—not simply a miner running unnoticed. Hackers Use SANSAR Linux Malware The deception targets NVIDIA Management Library, or NVML, the interface used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi . The attacker’s wrapper forwards requests to the genuine NVIDIA library, then changes selected results before returning them. GPU utilization becomes zero, while temperature and power readings are replaced with random values between 36–46 degrees Celsius and 100–200 watts. This makes apparently normal monitoring output unreliable. The GPU is not necessarily idle; the software reporting its activity has been altered. SANSAR can also rebuild and reinstall the wrapper from recovered source files, giving the operator a way to maintain the modified monitoring layer. Execution flow of SANSAR diagram (Source – Elastic) A separate kernel rootkit hides selected processes, files, and socket entries. It intercepts directory listings and other system operations, removing matching records or returning errors when tools inspect hidden processes. Similar Linux rootkit mining attacks have used kernel-level concealment, but this toolkit adds falsified GPU measurements to obscure resource use. SANSAR itself supervises publicly available mining software rather than performing every mining task internally. Its CPU branch uses XMRig, while its GPU branch launches SRBMiner-MULTI. The controller supplies pool addresses, wallet or login details, algorithms, and other settings. Elastic found no hardcoded fallback pool or wallet in those launch paths. Exposed Ray Jobs Enable Persistent Remote Access Recorded activity began with external probes on October 22, followed by a GPU inventory query on October 24. On October 25, the attacker submitted a Python reverse-shell job. Although the Ray head-node dashboard listened only on localhost, the job agent remained internet-accessible and accepted unauthenticated submissions. The initial shell ran under the account owning the Ray session. The attacker then added an SSH key for continued access. After obtaining root, the operator installed the toolkit, built its kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support, and added an early-boot loader. Elastic’s account does not explain the precise method used to obtain root. Control extends beyond mining. SANSAR communicates over Tor and supports interactive Bash shells, miner configuration changes, output forwarding, and TCP SYN traffic generation. Its shell setup suppresses saved command history. A separate backdoor retrieves its controller address from an Ethereum smart contract, then connects directly over TCP. This creates another route for shell access. Earlier Discord controlled mining campaigns also combined mining with remote control, although their communication methods differed from this intrusion. For defenders, Elastic highlights two priorities: check who can submit Ray jobs and verify whether GPU monitoring libraries have changed. items.title: Hackers Use 2,700 Passwords to Break Into Microsoft SQL Servers and Deploy Remote Access Malware
items.summary: A new campaign is guessing its way into internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server systems. The attackers use a list of more than 2,700 passwords and then install a cryptocurrency miner and a remote access trojan (RAT) on the hacked machines. The campaign has been running since at least early October 2026. Database servers hold valuable data, so they are a favorite target. This campaign scans for exposed servers, tries many logins, and runs commands that pull in more malware. Attackers have used the same basic approach for years, as seen when hackers were continuously attacking MS-SQL servers with scanner malware earlier this year. Researchers at Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs identified the malware and described the full infection chain in a report published on November 12, 2026. Analyst Xiaopeng Zhang noted that the campaign abuses T-SQL, Microsoft’s extension of the SQL language, to run commands on hacked servers. FortiGuard rates the severity as high. Hackers Use 2,700 Passwords to Break Into Microsoft SQL Servers The chain starts with a file named dllhost.exe. It is written in the Go language and packed with UPX to hide its contents. The name copies a real Windows process, which helps it blend in. The file contains the open-source Naabu port scanner. It contacts the attackers’ server, receives an IP range to scan, and checks each random address in that range for open TCP port 1433, the default port for SQL Server. Any open host is written to a file called Result.txt, and the malware then asks for the next range. The malware also downloads eight support files, including scripts named go.vbs and go.bat and a tool named dwm.exe. The infection chain of this malware campaign (Source – Fortinet) Despite its name, dwm.exe is a .NET program that guesses logins. It reads user names such as “sa” and “admin” from one file and tries more than 2,700 passwords from another, using up to 500 threads at once. Weak or reused passwords on exposed servers are what make this work. This is the same weakness behind older cases where criminals brute force MSSQL logins to drop ransomware. When a login works, the tool runs a file called 2018.sql on the server. Its commands turn on xp_cmdshell, a feature that lets SQL Server run Windows commands. They then download a program into the C:\Users\Public folder and name it Google.exe or payload.exe. They also create a daily scheduled task called Microsoft_UPDATES and drop another file, Secs.exe, into the Startup folder. The malware itself sets up a scheduled task that runs every 30 minutes and is named to look like a Microsoft Edge update. What the Miner and Gh0st RAT Do After the Break-In The downloader, Secs.exe, connects to an FTP server and pulls down more files, which it saves in the Temp folder and runs. It then creates another disguised Edge update task. Next it sends the victim’s public IP address, country, Windows version, processor, memory, user name and host name to the attackers. This registers the server in their system. One payload is MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, which is not an update at all. It is a Monero miner protected by two packers, Themida and a custom LZSS packer. It uses the server’s CPU to mine coins and connects to pools such as nanopool and kryptex. It also tells the attackers’ server when mining starts. The result is slow performance, higher power costs and wasted computing power for the victim. The second payload, winlogon.exe, is a variant of Gh0st RAT, which gives attackers remote control. It sets itself up three ways: a Run registry key, a Windows service and a scheduled task. Eight additional files to be downloaded (Source – Fortinet) It can log keystrokes, manage files, run a remote shell, wipe event logs and steal data from QQ, a Chinese messaging app. It also supports more than 30 control commands, and plugins add screen capture and remote desktop. The malware checks for 78 security product process names. Its command servers were offline when Fortinet tested it, so the team could only study the unpacked file. The same family has been seen before, when HiddenGh0st malware targeting MS-SQL servers was reported. Do not leave SQL Server open to the internet. Put it behind a firewall or VPN, and block port 1433 from outside networks. Use long, unique passwords, rename or disable the sa account, and lock accounts after repeated failures. Turn off xp_cmdshell unless you need it. Watch for new scheduled tasks that imitate Edge updates, unknown files in C:\Users\Public, and sudden spikes in CPU use. Recent reports of hijacking MS-SQL servers recently with C2 frameworks show that these servers remain a steady target. items.title: Citrix Patches 28 Security Vulnerabilities in NetScaler, Including a Critical Flaw in Default Installations
items.summary: Citrix has released fixes for 28 security flaws in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. One of them, CVE-2026-120868, affects every deployment in its default setup. Cloud Software Group published bulletin CTX697305 on November 12, 2026, and rated it Critical. CVE-2026-120868 is a memory overflow in packet processing . It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.3. Most NetScaler bugs need a specific feature turned on. This one does not. No extra setting is needed, so every unpatched appliance is vulnerable. The bug can cause unpredictable behavior or a denial-of-service. Because the attack needs no login and no user action, anyone who can reach the device over the network can try it. Almost all of the 28 flaws are memory bugs. They include buffer overflows, out-of-bounds writes, and a double free. Citrix says most can crash the device or make it behave oddly. Each one only matters if the matching feature is in use. The highest score, 9.5, belongs to CVE-2026-107412. It hits appliances set up as a Gateway, such as SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, or RDP Proxy, or as an AAA virtual server. Several other bugs score 9.3. They sit in areas like SMPP traffic, DNS and DNS-over-HTTPS, NetScaler Push, Email OTP login, Endpoint Analysis, and ICA proxy. Citrix Patches NetScaler Security Vulnerabilities Many others score 8.7 and touch SAML, WebAuth, LDAP, client-certificate login, HTTP/3, GSLB, Diameter, MQTT and RADIUS handling. A BGP routing flaw scores 7.7, but an attacker would need to be or fake a configured neighbor. Three flaws score 6.9. One of them, CVE-2026-111338, writes sensitive login data into the log file /var/log/httperror.log, so someone with local read access could see it. The bulletin covers customer-managed appliances. Versions 14.1 before 14.1-73.57 and 13.1 before 13.1-64.39 are affected. So are 14.1 FIPS before 14.1-73.58 FIPS, and 13.1 FIPS and NDcPP before 13.1-37.293. Citrix reports that Secure Private Access hybrid setups using NetScaler instances require upgrades, while Cloud Software Group is updating its managed cloud services and Adaptive Authentication; no workaround is available, and customers should install fixed builds immediately. items.title: Hackers Use Fake Purchase Order Emails to Deliver XLoader Malware Through Malicious Word Documents
items.summary: Hackers are sending fake purchase order emails to trick recipients into opening Word documents that deliver XLoader, an information-stealing malware. The attack uses an embedded document, an old Microsoft Equation Editor vulnerability, and several script stages to reach its final payload. What begins as a routine order confirmation can end with stolen browser data and additional malware on an infected computer. The lure fits everyday purchasing workflows, asking recipients to review prices, quantities, and shipping arrangements. Similar fake business order emails have delivered XLoader through script attachments, but this case uses a DOCX file to hide the next stage. The familiar business language gives employees a reason to open the attachment without questioning its contents. Researchers from ASEC identified the phishing activity and described the infection chain in a November 12 report. Their technical analysis of the campaign shows how a Word attachment leads to script execution, registry-based persistence, and an encrypted payload that ultimately runs in memory. The final malware is XLoader, with version information showing release 8.9. Hackers Use Fake Purchase Order Emails The sample email presents an order worth $144,744.50 and asks for shipment by the end of the following month. It tells the recipient to report pricing or quantity discrepancies before shipping. These details create a believable reason to inspect the attached purchase order while keeping attention on the supposed transaction rather than the document’s safety. Opening the attachment starts a chain inside Word. The DOCX contains a malicious Rich Text Format document, which Word processes through its “Import Content from Another Document” feature, known as altChunk. This feature provides the route into the embedded content; the code execution step then relies on CVE-2017-11882 in Microsoft Equation Editor. Phishing email body (Source – ASEC) While Word processes the RTF content, an embedded Object Linking and Embedding package writes a Visual Basic Script file into the temporary directory. A separate Equation Editor object exploits the vulnerability to execute that script through Windows Script Host. Earlier Equation Editor exploitation campaigns also used order-themed documents to distribute XLoader, although their filenames and delivery stages differed. The script contains Base64-encoded data, saves it locally, and launches an embedded first-stage PowerShell script. After decoding, the data contains three parts: a loader, an encrypted payload, and a second PowerShell script. This layered packaging places multiple execution steps between the original document and XLoader, rather than exposing the final malware directly inside the visible purchase order. Registry Persistence and In-Memory XLoader Execution The first PowerShell stage stores its execution path and script content in separate registry values. It also creates a current-user Run entry, allowing the stored script to execute again when the user signs in. This persistence mechanism means the attack does not depend solely on keeping the original Word document open after the initial compromise. Next, the first script decrypts the saved data and starts the secondary PowerShell stage. That script runs the loader and passes the encrypted payload as an argument. The loader applies an XOR operation to recover the payload and execute it in memory. Separate reporting on XLoader malware evasion techniques describes the family’s wider use of encryption and hidden communications, but those details should not be assumed for this sample. Command execution for the malicious VBS file embedded in the OLE object (Source – ASEC) ASEC identifies the final payload as an information stealer that collects computer details and browser data. It can also download additional malware, extending the risk beyond the first infection. The report does not name a threat actor, establish how many organizations received the emails, or confirm the total number of compromised systems. Defenders should verify unexpected purchase orders through a known contact and keep Office installations patched. Monitoring should connect suspicious document activity with script execution and registry changes, rather than treating each event separately. ASEC advises checking sender domains and attachments carefully. For this chain, the document-to-script transition and logon persistence provide useful investigation points alongside the published indicators. items.title: Hackers exploit exposed GeoVision CCTV software to disable Defender and deploy cryptominers
items.summary: Threat actors are abusing internet-exposed GeoVision surveillance software to break into corporate networks, disable Microsoft Defender, and quietly install cryptomining malware, according to new research from Huntress. The Huntress Security Operations Centre (SOC) began seeing the activity on 8 November, with most attacks landing between 8 and 10 November and activity continuing over the past week. So far, 13 organisations across a range of industries have been affected. GeoVision is a Taiwanese surveillance and access-control vendor. Every incident traced back to the same source: GeoStartupAgentService.exe, a GeoVision service that on many machines was running with full SYSTEM privileges. Searches of the victims’ external IP addresses on Shodan showed GeoVision devices or management interfaces sitting openly on the internet. Blinding the defences first Once the attackers had a foothold, the GeoVision service spawned a command shell that pulled down a chain of PowerShell scripts from an attacker-controlled server. Before installing their payload, the attackers worked to disarm the victim’s security tools. The scripts checked whether Microsoft Defender was running and downloaded a vulnerable kernel driver, wsftprm.sys (disguised as kvckiller.sys), which has previously been abused in Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attacks to tamper with antivirus. The attackers also used Image File Execution Options (IFEO), a legitimate Windows debugging feature, to hijack the Defender antivirus engine and Windows Security components. This redirected them to launch systray.exe instead, likely to stop the protections from starting at all. Persistent, and hard to take down With defences weakened, a final script dropped a custom loader written in Go, which reached out to infrastructure linked to the domain cctv-update[.]top. The domain was registered on 7 November, the day before the attacks began. The loader stands out for its resilience. It includes a BitTorrent Mainline DHT client and a PKARR resolver, which let it find the attacker’s current servers using a public key on the BitTorrent peer-to-peer network. That means the operator can move infrastructure without registering new domains, and taking down a single server won’t cut off access. On some machines, the loader created scheduled tasks named PackageUpdater and PackageUpdater_Startup to relaunch itself every 15 minutes and at boot. It then installed the XMRig cryptominer, disguised as ApplyUpdate.exe, to hijack the victims’ computing power. Cameras are part of the attack surface Huntress said the campaign is the latest in a series of incidents it has seen where attackers target camera systems. It urged organisations to treat camera management software as part of the enterprise attack surface, not as a separate building-security concern. Huntress recommends that organisations running GeoVision software: Remove unnecessary internet exposure of GeoVision devices and management interfaces, putting them behind a VPN or restricting access to trusted IP addresses. Investigate any unexpected command shells or PowerShell launched by GeoStartupAgentService.exe. Watch for outbound UDP DHT traffic (port 6881 or similar) from the GeoVision process WebCamServer.exe, DNS queries to public resolvers made by processes other than the system DNS client, and schtasks /Create commands launched by update.exe. Isolate any affected hosts and preserve evidence before removing files or changing configurations. The full advisory, including indicators of compromise and MITRE ATT&CK mappings, is available on the Huntress blog: https://www.huntress.com/blog/geovision-camera-software-xmrig-cryptominer

items.title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
items.summary: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever. Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling. You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects. Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway. How it works You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI , or REST API . In the dashboard , head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending. When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds. If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically. If you go to the dashboard , you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit. Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month. The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached. As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation . Here’s an example, but using the API: curl --fail-with-body --request POST \ "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API : cf billing spend-policies list cf billing spend-policies create cf billing spend-policies get cf billing spend-policies update cf billing spend-policies delete cf billing spend-policies audit list cf billing spend-policies activity list cf billing spend-policies create --body '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served. To resume service, you can: Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend. Disable or delete the blocking policy. Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires. That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon. Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next. How we built Spend Management As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch. Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event: Now let's dig deeper. Collecting and aggregating close to the source Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient. So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one. Let's look at a diagram. The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window. In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation. The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale. Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics. We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place. That lets us maintain its accumulated usage and apply included allowances without coordinating across pricing processors on every update. As you can see, we run different partitions in parallel, giving us a way to spread the work across accounts while keeping each account’s pricing state together. Also note that each partition keeps both a local state for fast access, and also a durable write-ahead logging (WAL) changelog on disk. This buys us: Less cross-partition coordination : each account’s usage and subscription state stay together. Consistent pricing : usage updates share the same allowance and accumulated-spend state. Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever.

Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling.

You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.

Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.

How it works

You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI, or REST API.

In the dashboard, head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending.

When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds.

If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically.

If you go to the dashboard, you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit.

Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month.

The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached.

As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation. Here’s an example, but using the API:

curl --fail-with-body --request POST \
  "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "Workers spending cap",
    "product_id": "workers",
    "enabled": true,
    "threshold_cents": 10000,
    "action": "usage_block",
    "notification_email": "me@example.com"
  }'

And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API:

cf billing spend-policies list
cf billing spend-policies create
cf billing spend-policies get
cf billing spend-policies update
cf billing spend-policies delete
cf billing spend-policies audit list
cf billing spend-policies activity list

cf billing spend-policies create --body '{
  "name": "Workers spending cap",
  "product_id": "workers",
  "enabled": true,
  "threshold_cents": 10000,
  "action": "usage_block",
  "notification_email": "me@example.com"
}'

Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served.

To resume service, you can:

  • Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend.
  • Disable or delete the blocking policy.
  • Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires.

That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon.

Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next.

How we built Spend Management

As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch.

Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event:

Now let's dig deeper.

Collecting and aggregating close to the source

Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient.

So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one.

Let's look at a diagram.

The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window.

In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation.

The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale.

Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing

The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics.

We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place. That lets us maintain its accumulated usage and apply included allowances without coordinating across pricing processors on every update.

  • Recoverability: durable state lets replacement processors rebuild and resume after failures, if necessary.

items.summary: A major Microsoft 365 outage disrupted cloud service access on November 12 and continued into November 13, 2026, as Microsoft worked to restore failing infrastructure. Microsoft confirmed that connectivity problems could affect users in any region, expanding the scope beyond its initial investigation into Exchange Online mailbox access in the Americas. The reported impact spans Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR, although the exact service and feature restrictions remain subject to Microsoft’s updated advisory. Administrators should check incident MO1550821 for that breakdown. Exchange Online mailbox connectivity is also being tracked separately under EX1550543. Microsoft has not confirmed that every customer is affected. We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026 Early findings pointed to heavy load across several regions. Microsoft later clarified that the pressure did not come from increased traffic. Instead, servers had unexpectedly become unavailable, leaving the remaining infrastructure to handle connections. Engineers began moving traffic across Microsoft’s worldwide systems to reduce pressure on the affected environment. The disruption follows other cloud availability incidents, including a Microsoft 365 outage affecting Teams, SharePoint and Copilot in July. That earlier incident involved a network configuration change. Microsoft has not established the same cause here, making it important to separate historical context from the current investigation. Failed Health Checks Complicate Recovery Microsoft identified failed automated health checks as a key part of the current problem. These checks determine whether servers remain available to handle requests. Investigators focused on a component responsible for processing server health, while testing a configuration change and restarting affected servers to bring capacity back online. According to Microsoft’s official incident updates , an alternative health check method allowed some servers to return to service. Engineers began applying that approach more widely and preparing automated recovery systems to detect and restart unresponsive machines. However, these measures did not immediately deliver the expected improvement. Microsoft subsequently found that a core process on affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, causing further capacity loss. Some restored servers initially remained stable, but later became unresponsive again when traffic reached them. That pattern complicated recovery because bringing servers online did not necessarily mean they could sustain normal use. Engineers paused deployments, shifted traffic onto alternate routes and reviewed whether reversing several recent configuration updates could speed recovery. Microsoft initially said it had not identified a recent change matching the start of the disruption. The later rollback assessment therefore remains a recovery option, not proof of the root cause. Security Visibility and Business Impact For security teams, reported Defender XDR disruption raises questions about access to alerts and investigations. A previous Microsoft Defender portal access incident showed how dashboard availability can interrupt security workflows. However, portal access problems alone do not establish that endpoint protection or background detection has stopped working. Administrators should follow EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center and use Microsoft’s public service status page when the admin center is unavailable. Microsoft’s public updates describe infrastructure failures and recovery work, rather than presenting evidence of a confirmed cyberattack behind this disruption. The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.

That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.

This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.

The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.

AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?

AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.

And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.

I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.

The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.

Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.

Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.

The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.

Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.

So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.

I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.

items.title: Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents to Breach 10 Organizations in Autonomous Cyberattacks
items.summary: Chinese-speaking hackers have used AI agents powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM to break into 10 organizations with very little human effort. The campaign ran in August and September 2026 and covered 25 operations against at least 19 targets. It shows how quickly autonomous AI cyberattacks are moving from theory into daily use. The attackers did not build anything new. They took a public, open-source penetration testing framework called Cairn and connected it to two Chinese AI models. They gave it a target and a goal, and the tool planned, ran and recorded each step by itself. A small team could therefore attack many organizations at once. Analysts at Unit42 identified the activity and track it as CL-STA-1238. They believe, with moderate confidence, that it is a China-linked intelligence collection effort. The targets were in semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy and civil society. Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents Cairn works through AI “agent workers.” Each worker reads and writes to a shared “blackboard,” where confirmed findings are saved as facts and next steps are saved as intents. The tool repeats a simple loop. In the Reason phase, the model reviews what it knows and decides what to try next. In the Explore phase, it carries out one action and logs the result. The loop stops when the goal is met, the options run out, or the operator steps in. Attacker-operated Cairn login page (Source – Unit42) For each target, the attackers only needed to enter the organization’s root domain and a one-line goal, often written in Chinese. One task said to “breach the target as fast as possible.” In one case, they also supplied VPN gateway addresses and shared group passwords gathered beforehand. The model then built its own plan of three to seven stages. These covered reconnaissance, web application exploitation, credential collection, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Of the 25 operations, 13 ran on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The attackers seem to have compared the models. They switched to the stronger V4 Pro when Flash failed against a hard target. Some runs lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no time limit set. The attackers also had little trouble with AI guardrails. Cairn’s default prompts already tell the model never to refuse a task. The attackers added a Chinese-language note claiming the work was an authorized security test, and they created an AUTHORIZATION.md file for each operation. Neither GLM nor DeepSeek refused. This is similar to a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent case that hit a European telecom provider earlier this month. Victims, Stolen Data and Warning Signs for Defenders Seven of the targets were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain. Three were defense-related, including a space technology company and a policy think tank. Four were human rights or civil society groups, such as a Canadian human-rights body and a U.S. teachers’ union. At an industry standards body, weak-password spraying gave the attackers dozens of valid credentials and access to internal directory data. They also overwrote a live standards-ballot document. At another organization, a brute-forced credential led to unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token. Cairn orchestration loop (Source – Unit42) A content management system flaw exposed more than one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes. An open registration endpoint leaked roughly 500 user records, including .mil and .gov accounts. Other cases involved employee data at a lithography maker, about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation company, and student data at an education nonprofit. The flaws behind these breaches were not new. They included authentication bypasses, insecure direct object references, mass-assignment privilege escalation, weak or default passwords, exposed cloud APIs and old public CVEs. AI raised the speed and reach of the work, not its difficulty. Other recent cases follow the same pattern, such as open-source ARTEX AI agents that automate Active Directory abuse. For defenders, the basics still work. Teams should use strong, unique passwords with phishing-resistant MFA, reduce internet-facing systems, patch known CVEs quickly and watch for noisy traffic from a single IP address. Unit 42 notes that Cairn generated hundreds of thousands of high-frequency requests from one origin. The researchers expect these campaigns to grow as open models with weak guardrails become more capable. Readers can also see how one hacker running 12 coordinated AI agents hit hundreds of targets, and how agents rebuild failed tools and keep going. items.title: Microsoft 365 Massive Outage – Fixes Fail as Restored Servers Keep Going Unresponsive
items.summary: Microsoft has yet to find a fix that holds for the global Microsoft 365 outage , which has now run for more than 10 hours. Servers that engineers bring back online are falling over again as soon as user traffic reaches them. The outage began on November 12, 2026, and continued through November 13. As we reported earlier , it started with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas. It then spread to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR users in any region. Microsoft’s latest status updates show the recovery has stalled. The company says it is running several workstreams in parallel to “address our current blocker” and return parts of its infrastructure to a healthy state. It has given no estimated time for full restoration. The incidents are tracked as EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Restored Servers Fail Again Under Load The core problem is that restarting servers does not keep them healthy. In an update on its Microsoft 365 Status account, Microsoft said restored servers “can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic.” The servers we returned to service can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic; we're analyzing diagnostic data to determine what's triggering the behavior. In parallel, we're temporarily limiting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in some… — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 13, 2026 Engineers are still analyzing diagnostic data to learn what triggers the behavior. Microsoft has not announced a root cause. With restarts failing to hold, the company has moved to three fallback measures: Traffic limiting. Microsoft is temporarily restricting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in some locations. Server rebuilds. A subset of affected servers is being rebuilt on a previous configuration, to test whether that stops them from going unresponsive. Traffic rerouting. Engineers are adjusting traffic protocols, redistributing load, and applying what Microsoft calls strategic traffic blocking. Microsoft says it sees partial recovery in regions where these traffic measures are in place. Partial recovery is not stable service, and users in those regions may still see intermittent failures. We've reviewed known impact scenarios and revised the list of impacted services and features, which can be viewed in the "more info" section of the communication MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as https://t.co/uFnnN6Svuf if the admin center is not available… — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 13, 2026 The rebuild on a previous configuration is the notable step. It suggests Microsoft suspects a recent change, though it has not confirmed one as the cause. Microsoft says it is seeing positive results from efforts to restart affected infrastructure and restore server availability amid the ongoing Microsoft 365 service disruption. The company is recovering impacted infrastructure in an isolated manner and closely monitoring performance to confirm stability before expanding restoration efforts more broadly. We’re seeing positive results with our efforts to restart affected infrastructure and recover server availability in an isolated manner. We’re actively monitoring the performance of these portions of infrastructure to verify stability, which we suspect will support improved… — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 13, 2026 Following these initial recovery efforts, Microsoft expects service availability to improve gradually as the restoration process expands across the affected infrastructure. Administrators can track further updates under incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center or through Microsoft’s alternative status update link . We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvement where possible to help support traffic in regions coming online. We’re continuing to monitor the results of changes applied so we can identify strategic actions that can help to improve service health across all affected regions.… — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 13, 2026 How the Outage Unfolded Microsoft first blamed elevated load across multiple regions. It later corrected that view: traffic had not increased, but a number of servers had unexpectedly dropped out, straining the rest. The servers were failing automated health checks, which decide whether a machine can take requests. Engineers paused all deployments, moved traffic to other parts of the worldwide infrastructure, and restarted the affected servers. Those steps did not work. Microsoft admitted its actions had “not provided the anticipated relief” and found that a core process on the servers was being overwhelmed. An alternative health check method brought some servers back, and they appeared stable at first. The latest updates confirm that stability did not last once traffic returned. Scale of the Impact Downdetector logged more than 120,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak, and reports came from 74 countries. Report volumes have since fallen as partial recovery took effect. Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna confirmed it was not caused by a security breach, Business Standard reported. Administrators should: Track MO1550821 and EX1550543 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, or use status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center will not load. Avoid resetting passwords, rebuilding Outlook profiles, or changing tenant settings in response to the errors. Expect intermittent access even in regions showing recovery, since Microsoft is deliberately blocking some traffic types. items.title: Hackers Use Windows Named Pipes and SMB to Spread Malware Across Isolated Government Networks
items.summary: A new espionage group is using Windows named pipes and the SMB file-sharing protocol to move malware through tightly separated networks. Positive Technologies calls the group StingyBasilisk. It has been active since at least April 2022. The attackers sat quietly inside the victim’s systems for a long time and posed as the organization’s own security tools. The team could not find out how the attackers first got in. It did find a large network of custom agents, all controlled through Windows named pipes. Named pipes are a normal Windows feature that lets programs talk to each other, so the traffic blends in with everyday activity. The stealth of the operation points to spying as the main goal. Analysts at Habr, where Positive Technologies published its incident response findings, noted that every malware sample was a DLL built to wait and then run its payload only in the memory of a Windows process. Nothing obvious is left on disk. The researchers also suspect the group runs its own command-and-control framework, and no known threat group has been reliably linked to it. Hackers Use Windows Named Pipes and SMB From February 2026, the attackers began spreading inside the victim’s network. They copied malware to target machines over SMB and placed the files in C:\Windows\Temp. They then started the files remotely with atexec, a tool from the Impacket toolkit that runs commands through the Windows Task Scheduler. The tool connects over SMB, opens the \pipe\atsvc pipe, and creates and runs a task right away. This is close to the way PsExec can be abused for remote execution. The task names looked like random GUIDs, which differs from the default name in the Impacket script. This is one small clue defenders can use to spot the activity. In this phase the attackers launched the CunningDoor loader, using rundll32 to run a signed SafeNet library that in turn loaded a malicious DLL. Reading 256 bytes of IP packet data (Source – Habr) Named pipes are also how the malware is controlled. The backdoors create pipes with predictable name patterns and wait for encrypted shellcode to arrive. This lets the attackers build a chain of infected hosts that pass commands to each other. A machine with no direct internet access can still be reached through a neighbor, which is how the group gets into isolated network segments and walks around perimeter defenses. Persistence Through COM Hijacking and Time Providers To survive reboots, the attackers used two uncommon methods. The first was COM hijacking for persistence . They changed the TreatAs registry key for the Network List Manager and Network Configuration objects. Whenever a process called these components, Windows loaded the attackers’ DLL instead, for example netprofmprox.dll, whose name is almost the same as the real netprofm.dll. The fake library still passes calls on to the real one. That keeps the system stable, so nothing crashes to give the attackers away. The malware also checks that it runs inside svchost.exe -k netsvcs and quits if it does not. This family is called SilentCOM. The second method abused the Windows Time service. The attackers added their own provider under the W32Time TimeProviders registry key and set Enabled to 1. At every boot, the service loaded their DLL inside svchost.exe with Local System rights. This loader, TediousLoader, opens raw sockets on every network adapter and reads incoming packets. A new espionage group is using Windows named pipes and the SMB file-sharing protocol to move malware through tightly separated networks. Positive Technologies calls the group StingyBasilisk.

It has been active since at least April 2022. The attackers sat quietly inside the victim’s systems for a long time and posed as the organization’s own security tools.

The team could not find out how the attackers first got in. It did find a large network of custom agents, all controlled through Windows named pipes.

Named pipes are a normal Windows feature that lets programs talk to each other, so the traffic blends in with everyday activity. The stealth of the operation points to spying as the main goal.

Analysts at Habr, where Positive Technologies published its incident response findings, noted that every malware sample was a DLL built to wait and then run its payload only in the memory of a Windows process.

Nothing obvious is left on disk. The researchers also suspect the group runs its own command-and-control framework, and no known threat group has been reliably linked to it.

Hackers Use Windows Named Pipes and SMB

From February 2026, the attackers began spreading inside the victim’s network. They copied malware to target machines over SMB and placed the files in C:\Windows\Temp.

They then started the files remotely with atexec, a tool from the Impacket toolkit that runs commands through the Windows Task Scheduler.

The tool connects over SMB, opens the \pipe\atsvc pipe, and creates and runs a task right away. This is close to the way PsExec can be abused for remote execution.

The task names looked like random GUIDs, which differs from the default name in the Impacket script. This is one small clue defenders can use to spot the activity.

In this phase the attackers launched the CunningDoor loader, using rundll32 to run a signed SafeNet library that in turn loaded a malicious DLL.

Reading 256 bytes of IP packet data (Source – Habr)

Named pipes are also how the malware is controlled. The backdoors create pipes with predictable name patterns and wait for encrypted shellcode to arrive.

This lets the attackers build a chain of infected hosts that pass commands to each other. A machine with no direct internet access can still be reached through a neighbor, which is how the group gets into isolated network segments and walks around perimeter defenses.

Persistence Through COM Hijacking and Time Providers

To survive reboots, the attackers used two uncommon methods. The first was COM hijacking for persistence. They changed the TreatAs registry key for the Network List Manager and Network Configuration objects.

Whenever a process called these components, Windows loaded the attackers’ DLL instead, for example netprofmprox.dll, whose name is almost the same as the real netprofm.dll.

The fake library still passes calls on to the real one. That keeps the system stable, so nothing crashes to give the attackers away. The malware also checks that it runs inside svchost.exe -k netsvcs and quits if it does not. This family is called SilentCOM.

The second method abused the Windows Time service. The attackers added their own provider under the W32Time TimeProviders registry key and set Enabled to 1.

At every boot, the service loaded their DLL inside svchost.exe with Local System rights. This loader, TediousLoader, opens raw sockets on every network adapter and reads incoming packets.

It looks for a secret signature, and the packet then tells it where to connect, listen, or bind. The code it receives is decrypted with AES-256 and run in memory.

This “sleep until a special packet arrives” design is similar to the one in the backdoor that stays silent until it is woken, which shows how popular the idea has become.

CunningDoor reaches its payload through DLL side-loading techniques. A legitimate, signed SafeNet DLL starts a malicious one, which decrypts shellcode from a file in the Temp folder.

A later tool, HenMapCaCon.dll, is written in Go and runs a TLS server over a named pipe. It can also pull files out of an infected system.

Positive Technologies watched named pipe traffic for the known name patterns and managed to capture and decrypt a payload. Teams can do the same.
