items.summary: Mostly a Barebone release: the Linux kernel module now loads the same agent that we upload through a GDB stub, Windows on arm64 under Parallels got a thorough going-over, and the original Windows 95 works. Beyond that there are Stalker fixes for recent glibc on arm64 from @cpruijsen , x86 relocation fixes from @tubibibo , module versions on Windows from @nblog , a round of QNX work from @KazWolfe , and a fix from @mrmacete for memory reads on iOS timing out. The package manager also installs into fresh projects again. Barebone Linux There used to be two Linux kernel agents: the image that the host uploads through a GDB stub, and the kernel module, which was a build of its own with its own injector. The module is now a small in-kernel loader for that very same image. It maps and relocates it, fills in the kernel addresses from kallsyms, and hands it the configuration the host would. The injector that lived in the module moved into the shared agent, with its prctl() channel, process memory operations, thread spawning into a target’s thread group, and cloaking with its /proc hooks, so both ways into the kernel get all of it. Struct offsets come from the kernel headers, falling back to BTF. @dystopia4096 reported that injecting into a process panicked the kernel on a Pixel 7 running a 6.1 kernel, with an analysis tracing it to the detach_pid() signature that changed in Linux 6.15. The agent now picks the right one at runtime, from whether free_pids() exists. Thanks for the excellent report! More kernels and configurations work as a result of this round: On x86 kernels from 6.2 to 6.14, the current task, preempt count and top of the stack are members of struct pcpu_hot rather than per-CPU variables of their own, which left the agent without a current task. On arm64, a thread started from the kernel side kept the vector lengths of the kernel thread it began as, so once it used SVE the kernel killed its thread group. It now gets the SVE and SME lengths of the leader. Wherever the agent is entered without a call, the stack now looks the way a call would have left it. Code relying on alignment used to fault, such as musl’s fstatat() on x86_64 Alpine, which made every lstat() from an injected agent crash. Stopping the agent could corrupt the kernel, as the fault handler’s uninstall wrote back the expected prologue of fixup_exception() even when install had found a different one and left it alone. An idle agent is now actually idle. Every waiter shared one wait queue and every wake woke them all, so each GLib lock released in a hook on a hot kernel path woke the idle worker, some ninety times a second on Android. Wakes now only reach the waiters of their token. And a wait without a timeout gave up after a second, and GLib’s lock waits after a millisecond; they now sleep until woken, as TASK_IDLE , so a long sleep neither adds to the load nor looks hung. Windows Windows on arm64 under Parallels took a string of fixes. Windows leaves T1SZ at 17, making the first translation table 2 KiB, so its address need not be aligned to a granule, and our mask assumed it was. Address translation stopped at level 3, misreading blocks and returning an address for an unmapped page. The Parallels stub refuses to read a mapped page whose access flag is clear, which Windows leaves that way on pages it has not touched in a while, such as the kernel’s export directory, so those are now read through the page tables, using the stub’s monitor for the MMU registers and physical memory. The stub also single-steps a processor told to continue alone, without ever reporting the stop, so we continue all of them. On the agent side, the process list is found from the loaded modules where the host hasn’t named the list head, the agent injected into a process can start threads there and not only in the kernel, and its fault handler is aligned so that a process with Control Flow Guard doesn’t end itself when calling it. Module.version now works for modules in Windows processes. And at the other end of the timeline, the original release of Windows 95 hung, as the address of VWIN32’s thread slot was that of OSR2. It is now read out of VWIN32_GetContextHandle() , like we already did for KERNEL32. GDB Stops are handled asynchronously, so one that arrived just before the target was resumed could finish being handled afterward, and mark the running target as stopped. Such stops are now dropped. Stalker Christopher found that following a thread that calls pthread_create() crashed on arm64 Linux with glibc 2.38 or newer. glibc starts threads with clone3 there, which the arm64 backend didn’t know about, so the new thread kept running with its parent’s execution context and stack. With that fixed, the next thread creation aborted in free() : the minimal prolog only saved q0 through q7 , while delivering a compile event clobbered q31 , which glibc’s TLS setup keeps a constant in. All 32 vector registers are now saved, as on x86. Thanks! x86 tubibibo fixed two relocation issues. LOOP , LOOPE and LOOPNE were copied verbatim, leaving their displacement relative to the wrong address, and Stalker lost control when they were taken. They are now rewritten like JECXZ , which also no longer turns into JRCXZ on x86_64. And a jump to the very next instruction ended relocation, so Interceptor.attach() failed on a short block ending in one, as @astro3141 reported. Relocation now continues past it. Thanks! Windows Module.version was always null on Windows. @nblog implemented it by parsing the file version out of the module’s version resource, without relying on version.dll. Thanks! While in there, I hardened the PE parser against truncated and malformed files, which could make it read past the end of the data. QNX Kaz has been testing Frida on QNX, on both a physical ARM device and an x86 VM, and sent a round of fixes: Interceptor on ARM now honors the function’s size, so a 4-byte function such as _exit() , a lone BL into __exit() , no longer gets an 8-byte redirect that clobbers the function following it. It also prefers a trampoline within reach of a 4-byte branch over a code deflector, which patches a module’s ELF header, in line with x86 and arm64. Replacing an execute-in-place page with a private copy now clears the cache before resuming, as threads could otherwise fetch stale instructions, and keeps signals masked meanwhile. The injector’s ARM payload encoded calls relative to the local buffer rather than where it would run in the target. Enumerating sections and relocations no longer walks past the section details when loading them failed, as for an execute-in-place image. The injector supports x86, with GLib and libunwind changes to match. Thanks! iOS Francesco tracked down memory reads through debugserver that timed out after 30 seconds. Replies are told apart from asynchronous notifications by their first byte, so a binary reply starting with S , T , W , X or O was taken for a stop, exit or console output notification, and the read never got its answer. A memory read’s reply is now claimed by the read while it is the oldest request awaiting one. Thanks! Package manager Every install into a fresh project failed with a complaint about a missing package.json , before downloading anything. The probe for an existing installation didn’t catch the error type that file operations throw since the Efni split in 17.25.0. Build Francesco found that top-level builtin options such as strip never reached our compat builds, resulting in a stripped arm64 Gadget slice despite –enable-symbols . A related spelling quirk in Meson’s option store kept the resolved version from being passed along, and made the parent’s assets option replace the sub-build’s. And in a shared build, idund is now installed beside the other assets, where the daemon locator looks for it. Enjoy! The package manager also installs into fresh projects again.

Barebone Linux

There used to be two Linux kernel agents: the image that the host uploads through a GDB stub, and the kernel module, which was a build of its own with its own injector. The module is now a small in-kernel loader for that very same image. It maps and relocates it, fills in the kernel addresses from kallsyms, and hands it the configuration the host would.

The injector that lived in the module moved into the shared agent, with its prctl() channel, process memory operations, thread spawning into a target’s thread group, and cloaking with its /proc hooks, so both ways into the kernel get all of it. Struct offsets come from the kernel headers, falling back to BTF.

@dystopia4096 reported that injecting into a process panicked the kernel on a Pixel 7 running a 6.1 kernel, with an analysis tracing it to the detach_pid() signature that changed in Linux 6.15. The agent now picks the right one at runtime, from whether free_pids() exists. Thanks for the excellent report!

More kernels and configurations work as a result of this round:

  • On x86 kernels from 6.2 to 6.14, the current task, preempt count and top of the stack are members of struct pcpu_hot rather than per-CPU variables of their own, which left the agent without a current task.
  • On arm64, a thread started from the kernel side kept the vector lengths of the kernel thread it began as, so once it used SVE the kernel killed its thread group. It now gets the SVE and SME lengths of the leader.
  • Wherever the agent is entered without a call, the stack now looks the way a call would have left it. Code relying on alignment used to fault, such as musl’s fstatat() on x86_64 Alpine, which made every lstat() from an injected agent crash.
  • Stopping the agent could corrupt the kernel, as the fault handler’s uninstall wrote back the expected prologue of fixup_exception() even when install had found a different one and left it alone.

An idle agent is now actually idle. Every waiter shared one wait queue and every wake woke them all, so each GLib lock released in a hook on a hot kernel path woke the idle worker, some ninety times a second on Android. Wakes now only reach the waiters of their token. And a wait without a timeout gave up after a second, and GLib’s lock waits after a millisecond; they now sleep until woken, as TASK_IDLE, so a long sleep neither adds to the load nor looks hung.

Windows

Windows on arm64 under Parallels took a string of fixes. Windows leaves T1SZ at 17, making the first translation table 2 KiB, so its address need not be aligned to a granule, and our mask assumed it was. Address translation stopped at level 3, misreading blocks and returning an address for an unmapped page. The Parallels stub refuses to read a mapped page whose access flag is clear, which Windows leaves that way on pages it has not touched in a while, such as the kernel’s export directory, so those are now read through the page tables, using the stub’s monitor for the MMU registers and physical memory. The stub also single-steps a processor told to continue alone, without ever reporting the stop, so we continue all of them.

On the agent side, the process list is found from the loaded modules where the host hasn’t named the list head, the agent injected into a process can start threads there and not only in the kernel, and its fault handler is aligned so that a process with Control Flow Guard doesn’t end itself when calling it. Module.version now works for modules in Windows processes.

And at the other end of the timeline, the original release of Windows 95 hung, as the address of VWIN32’s thread slot was that of OSR2. It is now read out of VWIN32_GetContextHandle(), like we already did for KERNEL32.

GDB

Stops are handled asynchronously, so one that arrived just before the target was resumed could finish being handled afterward, and mark the running target as stopped. Such stops are now dropped.

Stalker

Christopher found that following a thread that calls pthread_create() crashed on arm64 Linux with glibc 2.38 or newer. glibc starts threads with clone3 there, which the arm64 backend didn’t know about, so the new thread kept running with its parent’s execution context and stack. With that fixed, the next thread creation aborted in free(): the minimal prolog only saved q0 through q7, while delivering a compile event clobbered q31, which glibc’s TLS setup keeps a constant in. All 32 vector registers are now saved, as on x86. Thanks!

x86

tubibibo fixed two relocation issues. LOOP, LOOPE and LOOPNE were copied verbatim, leaving their displacement relative to the wrong address, and Stalker lost control when they were taken. They are now rewritten like JECXZ, which also no longer turns into JRCXZ on x86_64. And a jump to the very next instruction ended relocation, so Interceptor.attach() failed on a short block ending in one, as @astro3141 reported. Relocation now continues past it. Thanks!

Windows

Module.version was always null on Windows. @nblog implemented it by parsing the file version out of the module’s version resource, without relying on version.dll. Thanks! While in there, I hardened the PE parser against truncated and malformed files, which could make it read past the end of the data.

QNX

Kaz has been testing Frida on QNX, on both a physical ARM device and an x86 VM, and sent a round of fixes:

  • Interceptor on ARM now honors the function’s size, so a 4-byte function such as _exit(), a lone BL into __exit(), no longer gets an 8-byte redirect that clobbers the function following it. It also prefers a trampoline within reach of a 4-byte branch over a code deflector, which patches a module’s ELF header, in line with x86 and arm64.
  • Replacing an execute-in-place page with a private copy now clears the cache before resuming, as threads could otherwise fetch stale instructions, and keeps signals masked meanwhile.
  • The injector’s ARM payload encoded calls relative to the local buffer rather than where it would run in the target.
  • Enumerating sections and relocations no longer walks past the section details when loading them failed, as for an execute-in-place image.
  • The injector supports x86, with GLib and libunwind changes to match.

Thanks!

iOS

Francesco tracked down memory reads through debugserver that timed out after 30 seconds. Replies are told apart from asynchronous notifications by their first byte, so a binary reply starting with S, T, W, X or O was taken for a stop, exit or console output notification, and the read never got its answer. A memory read’s reply is now claimed by the read while it is the oldest request awaiting one. Thanks!

Package manager

Every install into a fresh project failed with a complaint about a missing package.json, before downloading anything. The probe for an existing installation didn’t catch the error type that file operations throw since the Efni split in 17.25.0.

Francesco found that top-level builtin options such as strip never reached our compat builds, resulting in a stripped arm64 Gadget slice despite –enable-symbols. A related spelling quirk in Meson’s option store kept the resolved version from being passed along, and made the parent’s assets option replace the sub-build’s. And in a shared build, idund is now installed beside the other assets, where the daemon locator looks for it.

items.title: Google pushes second Chrome update this week
items.summary: On November 11, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.78 for Linux . It includes 83 security fixes, five of which are rated Critical—the highest severity level. This update came out only two days after the previous one. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. items.title: US Freezes $2.7 Billion Stolen by North Korean Hackers in Massive $6 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
items.summary: The US government has frozen more than $2.7 billion of the crypto stolen from Binance on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI says North Korea took over $6 billion in that theft. Court orders already allow US officials to seize or hold more than $1.2 billion of the frozen funds. The Justice Department announced the action on November 12, along with a separate move against a North Korean scam called FaceStealer. The FBI blames a North Korean group it calls TraderTraitor for the Binance theft. As our earlier report on the FBI’s attribution of the Binance theft noted, the bureau tied the case to North Korea within days. The FBI, Secret Service, and IRS Criminal Investigation say the thieves are mostly turning stolen funds into Ethereum. They then plan to push the money through DeFi tools and instant swap services to hide its path. The Justice Department says its National Security Division, Criminal Division, and the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia worked with crypto service providers to stop the money. Officials say the thieves keep moving funds through bridges, mixers, and exchanges. The FBI has asked service providers to block any transfers linked to the addresses the hackers use. Binance itself reported that customers were made whole. Reports say the exchange covered losses from its SAFU emergency fund, and early findings point to a compromised engineer’s laptop. US Freezes $2.7B in North Korean Crypto Heist Funds The Justice Department stressed that FaceStealer is a different campaign from the Binance theft . The FBI says it has cost victims more than $400 million in 18 months. It blames groups tracked as Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, BlueNoroff, APT38, and Stardust Chollima. Agents seized cloud servers used in the scheme, along with over 900 secretly recorded victim webcam videos. The trick starts with a hijacked account, often on Telegram. The hackers message the victim’s contacts and propose a video call. They then send a link to a fake Zoom or Teams site. Inside, the target sees a recorded video of someone they know, which makes the call look real. The malware campaign uses fake meeting audio-fix prompts to trick victims into installing cookie stealers, keyloggers, screen-capture tools, and backdoors, while stolen webcam footage fuels further fake meetings. Some attacks have used AI to make deepfake videos of well-known crypto figures. The FBI says the scheme still mostly relies on real stolen videos. Hackers have also waited months, or even more than a year, to drain wallets, watching balances grow. The FBI warns that the same trick now targets open-source maintainers. Earlier this year, hackers lured the maintainer of a popular JavaScript library into a fake Teams call and infected his computer. They then tried to add bad dependencies to a library with tens of millions of weekly downloads. Quick detection stopped it. This fits a wider pattern. Our coverage of UNC1069, which used fake Zoom and Teams meetings , showed the same fake error and copy-and-paste step. The FBI’s advice is simple. Join calls through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code instead of clicking links. Keep your webcam off until you can see and hear the person who invited you. Never paste commands into a terminal to fix a meeting problem. Confirm invites through a second channel, and turn on multifactor authentication for Telegram, Slack, and similar apps. Keep only small amounts in browser wallets, and never store seed phrases on your devices. If you think you were hit, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device, change passwords, log out all sessions, warn your contacts, and report it at IC3.gov with the keyword “FaceStealer.” The freeze shows that fast action can save stolen funds. The FaceStealer case shows that one convincing video call can still start the next big theft. items.title: CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines: Will Your AI System Need an Independent Audit?
items.summary: Picture a customer-support chatbot at a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. It answers questions about orders and returns. It runs on a third-party large language model. Nobody thinks of it as high-risk. Now the product team gives it one new permission: it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 without human sign-off. It's a small feature that saves agents hours a week. Under the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines that CERT-In issued on 4 November 2026, that one change can be enough to move the chatbot into a higher risk tier. And the tier decides how the system gets audited, how often, and by whom. The 107-page framework scores every AI system on eight risk factors. Most coverage so far has stopped at "four risk tiers, from low to critical." This post goes further: it explains how the scoring actually works, walks through the chatbot example factor by factor, and sets out what security teams should do now. Key Takeaways CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines (v1.0, 4 November 2026) cover AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, plus systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users. Every AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight risk factors. The total (8–32) sets one of four tiers, and the tier sets audit depth, frequency and independence. From Tier 2 upward, the minimum requirement includes an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation. Giving an AI system the ability to act, such as issuing refunds or calling tools, raises its autonomy score and is a named escalation trigger. AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, with 180-day log retention, in line with CERT-In's existing 2022 Directions. What CERT-In Issued and Who It Covers The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines set a common, risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their full lifecycle. CERT-In lists the document on its official guidelines page under reference CISG-2026-04. Source: CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, cover page. The scope is deliberately wide. It covers AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated by organizations in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. That brings in global AI-as-a-Service providers and SaaS platforms selling into India, not just Indian companies. It also doesn't matter where the model came from. The guidelines say AI systems stay in audit scope regardless of model origin, ownership, or delivery mechanism . Internally built models, proprietary vendor models, open-weight models, and models consumed through an API are all covered. If you can't get evidence from your vendor, that's recorded as a scope limitation, because the absence of access is not treated as evidence of conformity. Scope and exclusions · CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Sections 4.4–4.9 There are three narrow exclusions: Academic research AI that doesn't make decisions about individuals and isn't in production. It enters full scope once it moves to a pilot. Purely rule-based automation , such as traditional RPA with no machine learning. Hybrid systems that mix rules and ML are in scope. Consumer personal use , such as an individual using a photo-editing app. The providers of those tools remain in scope. Small companies get some relief, but only for low-risk systems. MSMEs and startups can use simplified self-assessment for Tier 1 systems. For Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems, the guidelines state there is no proportionality exemption: the full requirements apply regardless of organizational size. Is It Mandatory? The honest answer is: partly, and probably more so over time. The document is issued as guidelines and doesn't state a penalty or a compliance deadline. But it is written in mandatory language ("shall") and sets minimum audit requirements for each tier. Three things give it teeth in practice: It plugs into rules that are already binding. The six-hour incident reporting window and 180-day log retention come from CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 under Section 70B of the IT Act. The new guidelines bring AI incidents squarely into that regime: AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours. Regulators are named as intended users. The document lists RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and TRAI among the bodies it is written for. If a sectoral regulator adopts it, the tiers become obligations for banks, brokers, insurers and telecom operators. Buyers will ask for it. Government tenders and enterprise customers already demand CERT-In empaneled audit reports for traditional systems. Expect AI audit evidence to show up in procurement questionnaires next. For security leaders, the practical takeaway is to treat the framework as the benchmark your AI systems will be judged against, whether by a regulator, a customer or an auditor. How the Eight-Factor Risk Score Works Each AI system is scored from 1 (low) to 4 (critical) on eight inherent-risk factors, and the scores are added up. Organizations must score what the system can actually do, without taking credit for controls they claim to have in place. Factor What it asks F1: Impact severity How bad is the consequence of a wrong, compromised or unsafe output? F2: Autonomy and actionability What actions, tool calls or decisions can the AI take before a human approves? F3: Data sensitivity How sensitive is the data it processes, from public to biometric or classified? F4: Scale and exposure How many users, transactions or systems does it reach? F5: Reversibility How easily can the damage from a bad output or action be undone? F6: Sector criticality Does it support an essential, regulated or critical-infrastructure function? F7: Adversarial exposure Is it internal, internet-facing, or in an actively targeted environment? F8: Complexity and auditability How opaque is the model and its dependencies? Missing evidence can't justify a low score. The total maps to a tier, and the tier sets the minimum audit requirement: Score Tier Minimum audit requirement 8–12 Tier 1 (Low) Self-assessment or basic internal review, reviewed annually 13–19 Tier 2 (Moderate) Documented internal audit, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled auditing organization at least annually 20–26 Tier 3 (High) Periodic independent third-party audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization, every six months where risk or material change warrants 27–32 Tier 4 (Critical) Independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization with continuous monitoring The score isn't the final word. The guidelines list escalation triggers that can push a system up a tier regardless of its total. They include AI that can autonomously execute code, transactions, or external communications; AI with privileged access to production systems or sensitive data; and AI that can't be reliably interrupted, rolled back, or placed in a safe state. Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Section 5.4, page 25. Two more rules matter. Auditors must validate your tier independently, and where their assessment is higher than yours, the higher tier applies for scoping. And a tier can only be lowered after a documented reassessment shows a sustained drop in risk, approved by the organization's designated risk authority. The Chatbot That Jumps a Tier The same chatbot lands in Tier 2 when it only answers questions, and in Tier 3 once it can issue refunds. Here is an illustrative scoring using the calibration guide in Section 5.3 of the guidelines. Version A answers questions, checks order status through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over help articles and order history, and hands refunds to human agents. Version B is the same bot, but it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 on its own. Factor Version A: answers only Version B: issues refunds Why it changes F1: Impact severity 2 2 A wrong answer or a single bad refund is still limited and recoverable F2: Autonomy 2 3 Version B initiates consequential actions instead of advising a human F3: Data sensitivity 2 3 Refunds bring payment and financial data into play F4: Scale and exposure 3 3 Large-scale, customer-facing in both cases F5: Reversibility 2 3 Money paid out to the wrong account is costly and slow to recover F6: Sector criticality 2 2 An important business function, not critical infrastructure F7: Adversarial exposure 3 3 Internet-facing, so anyone can send it hostile prompts F8: Complexity 3 3 A third-party LLM is partially opaque to the deploying company Total 19 (Tier 2) 22 (Tier 3) Source: Illustrative scoring · tier bands and minimum audits from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Table 11 Three factor changes add three points, enough to cross from the top of Tier 2 into Tier 3. Two things stand out. First, even the "harmless" Version A sits at the top of Tier 2. That already means a documented internal audit, a simplified AI impact assessment, AI threat modelling and API security testing, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization at least annually. Many companies running customer-facing LLMs may not realize they're here. Second, Version B doesn't just cross a score threshold. Its ability to initiate transactions is also a named escalation trigger, and an internet-facing bot that can move money is an obvious prompt-injection target. Moving to Tier 3 adds a comprehensive AI impact assessment, validation independent of the development team, a comprehensive AI security assessment with VAPT, a formal AI Governance Committee, and audits as often as every six months. Note: This scoring is illustrative. Actual tiers depend on each system's real capabilities and context, and auditors will reach their own assessment. What Auditors Will Test Your AI For Section 9 of the guidelines adds dedicated requirements for generative AI, RAG, agentic, multimodal, and multi-agent systems. These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using: Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Table 16, page 63. Source: Refund chatbot attack surface · threats from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Section 9.2 Mapped onto the refund chatbot, each component becomes a separate test case, and the leaked-credential risk sits outside the system entirely CERT-In takes prompt injection seriously enough to apply it to auditors too. Picture a customer-support chatbot at a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. It answers questions about orders and returns. It runs on a third-party large language model. Nobody thinks of it as high-risk. 

Now the product team gives it one new permission: it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 without human sign-off. It's a small feature that saves agents hours a week. 

Under the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines that CERT-In issued on 4 November 2026, that one change can be enough to move the chatbot into a higher risk tier. And the tier decides how the system gets audited, how often, and by whom. 

The 107-page framework scores every AI system on eight risk factors. Most coverage so far has stopped at "four risk tiers, from low to critical." This post goes further: it explains how the scoring actually works, walks through the chatbot example factor by factor, and sets out what security teams should do now. 

Key Takeaways 

  • CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines (v1.0, 4 November 2026) cover AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, plus systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users. 

  • Every AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight risk factors. The total (8–32) sets one of four tiers, and the tier sets audit depth, frequency and independence. 

  • From Tier 2 upward, the minimum requirement includes an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation. 

  • Giving an AI system the ability to act, such as issuing refunds or calling tools, raises its autonomy score and is a named escalation trigger. 

  • AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, with 180-day log retention, in line with CERT-In's existing 2022 Directions. 

What CERT-In Issued and Who It Covers 

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines set a common, risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their full lifecycle. CERT-In lists the document on its official guidelines page under reference CISG-2026-04. 

Source: CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, cover page.

The scope is deliberately wide. It covers AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated by organizations in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. That brings in global AI-as-a-Service providers and SaaS platforms selling into India, not just Indian companies. 

It also doesn't matter where the model came from. The guidelines say AI systems stay in audit scope regardless of model origin, ownership, or delivery mechanism. Internally built models, proprietary vendor models, open-weight models, and models consumed through an API are all covered. If you can't get evidence from your vendor, that's recorded as a scope limitation, because the absence of access is not treated as evidence of conformity. 

Scope and exclusions · CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Sections 4.4–4.9 

There are three narrow exclusions: 

  • Academic research AI that doesn't make decisions about individuals and isn't in production. It enters full scope once it moves to a pilot. 

  • Purely rule-based automation, such as traditional RPA with no machine learning. Hybrid systems that mix rules and ML are in scope. 

  • Consumer personal use, such as an individual using a photo-editing app. The providers of those tools remain in scope. 

Small companies get some relief, but only for low-risk systems. MSMEs and startups can use simplified self-assessment for Tier 1 systems. For Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems, the guidelines state there is no proportionality exemption: the full requirements apply regardless of organizational size. 

Is It Mandatory? 

The honest answer is: partly, and probably more so over time. The document is issued as guidelines and doesn't state a penalty or a compliance deadline. But it is written in mandatory language ("shall") and sets minimum audit requirements for each tier. 

Three things give it teeth in practice: 

  • It plugs into rules that are already binding. The six-hour incident reporting window and 180-day log retention come from CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 under Section 70B of the IT Act. The new guidelines bring AI incidents squarely into that regime: AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours. 

  • Regulators are named as intended users. The document lists RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and TRAI among the bodies it is written for. If a sectoral regulator adopts it, the tiers become obligations for banks, brokers, insurers and telecom operators. 

  • Buyers will ask for it. Government tenders and enterprise customers already demand CERT-In empaneled audit reports for traditional systems. Expect AI audit evidence to show up in procurement questionnaires next. 

For security leaders, the practical takeaway is to treat the framework as the benchmark your AI systems will be judged against, whether by a regulator, a customer or an auditor. 

How the Eight-Factor Risk Score Works 

Each AI system is scored from 1 (low) to 4 (critical) on eight inherent-risk factors, and the scores are added up. Organizations must score what the system can actually do, without taking credit for controls they claim to have in place. 

Factor  What it asks  F1: Impact severity  How bad is the consequence of a wrong, compromised or unsafe output?  F2: Autonomy and actionability  What actions, tool calls or decisions can the AI take before a human approves?  F3: Data sensitivity  How sensitive is the data it processes, from public to biometric or classified?  F4: Scale and exposure  How many users, transactions or systems does it reach?  F5: Reversibility  How easily can the damage from a bad output or action be undone?  F6: Sector criticality  Does it support an essential, regulated or critical-infrastructure function?  F7: Adversarial exposure  Is it internal, internet-facing, or in an actively targeted environment?  F8: Complexity and auditability  How opaque is the model and its dependencies? Missing evidence can't justify a low score. 

The total maps to a tier, and the tier sets the minimum audit requirement: 

Score  Tier  Minimum audit requirement  8–12  Tier 1 (Low)  Self-assessment or basic internal review, reviewed annually  13–19  Tier 2 (Moderate)  Documented internal audit, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled auditing organization at least annually  20–26  Tier 3 (High)  Periodic independent third-party audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization, every six months where risk or material change warrants  27–32  Tier 4 (Critical)  Independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization with continuous monitoring 

The score isn't the final word. The guidelines list escalation triggers that can push a system up a tier regardless of its total. They include AI that can autonomously execute code, transactions, or external communications; AI with privileged access to production systems or sensitive data; and AI that can't be reliably interrupted, rolled back, or placed in a safe state.

Two more rules matter. Auditors must validate your tier independently, and where their assessment is higher than yours, the higher tier applies for scoping. And a tier can only be lowered after a documented reassessment shows a sustained drop in risk, approved by the organization's designated risk authority. 

The Chatbot That Jumps a Tier 

The same chatbot lands in Tier 2 when it only answers questions, and in Tier 3 once it can issue refunds. Here is an illustrative scoring using the calibration guide in Section 5.3 of the guidelines. 

Version A answers questions, checks order status through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over help articles and order history, and hands refunds to human agents. Version B is the same bot, but it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 on its own. 

Factor  Version A: answers only  Version B: issues refunds  Why it changes  F1: Impact severity  2  2  A wrong answer or a single bad refund is still limited and recoverable  F2: Autonomy  2  3  Version B initiates consequential actions instead of advising a human  F3: Data sensitivity  2  3  Refunds bring payment and financial data into play  F4: Scale and exposure  3  3  Large-scale, customer-facing in both cases  F5: Reversibility  2  3  Money paid out to the wrong account is costly and slow to recover  F6: Sector criticality  2  2  An important business function, not critical infrastructure  F7: Adversarial exposure  3  3  Internet-facing, so anyone can send it hostile prompts  F8: Complexity  3  3  A third-party LLM is partially opaque to the deploying company  Total  19 (Tier 2)  22 (Tier 3)

Three factor changes add three points, enough to cross from the top of Tier 2 into Tier 3.

Note: This scoring is illustrative. Actual tiers depend on each system's real capabilities and context, and auditors will reach their own assessment.

items.title: Detection Engineering: Implementing Detection-as-Code in an Existing Environment: Part 3 – Validation and Future Possibilities
items.summary: In Part 2, we described how we restructured the data to move all detection data into the new repository while preserving the existing Git history. In this third part, we examine data quality and the use of the data beyond the internal needs of the Detection Engineering team. We cover how systematic validation improved data quality, the first practical uses of the consolidated data, larger planned initiatives, and future opportunities to further improve and automate the Detection Engineering process. Consistency Validation At this point, all detection data had been successfully consolidated in the new repository. The format of the different files was largely kept unchanged to make the migration as easy as possible for detection developers and to avoid introducing additional friction. This also means that some information is stored in multiple files. For example, platform and severity levels are stored in both the metadata file and the implementation, while title and description are stored in the metadata file, the implementation, and the Atomic Red Team test definition. This is not inherently problematic; the data had been structured this way for a long time. However, it creates issues when the different files contain inconsistent values. If the metadata file states a different severity from that in the actual implementation, analyses and reports based on the metadata files are incorrect. Therefore, such inconsistencies needed to be identified and corrected, and we needed to ensure that no new inconsistencies would be introduced into the repository. To accomplish this, a validator was implemented. This validator contains numerous test cases that check files against defined requirements. These checks cover different questions: Whether files are parseable, preventing malformed files from breaking other scripts and automations. Whether files fulfil the defined schema, identifying missing, misspelled, or surplus keys. Whether values stored in multiple files are consistent. The checks are divided into different levels: required : These checks must always pass. required_on_change : These checks must pass when a detection is modified; for existing, unchanged detections, they are considered optional. optional : These checks create remarks for the developer but do not block a change. The differentiation between these levels makes the initial improvement of consistency manageable. While some issues need to be fixed before the data can be relied upon, such as severity values, MITRE ATT&CK IDs, and platforms, other data should be consistent long-term but would require too much effort to correct in a single step. Their inconsistency does not cause immediate problems, for example where Atomic Red Team test cases do not match a naming schema. These non-urgent checks become mandatory once a developer modifies the affected detection; until then, they remain optional. Furthermore, there are scenarios in which fields that are usually identical differ for legitimate reasons. For example, some descriptions contain variables in the implementation that are populated in the Splunk UI, while the description in the metadata document remains generic. The validator is built as a library that is used in two ways. Firstly, it is available as a CLI tool. This tool has parameters that define which levels of checks to report. With this tool, we identified inconsistencies and corrected them manually. This sometimes required research in old tickets to determine which of two values for a field was correct, as an error could have been introduced either when defining the metadata file or when implementing the detection. Secondly, validation is integrated into the development process through CI pipelines. When a pull request is opened, the CI pipeline runs the validation checks on the detection folders included in the pull request changeset. The result and detailed output are displayed in a GitHub check in the pull request to provide direct feedback to the detection developer. If any required or required_on_change checks fail, the pull request is automatically blocked from merging. When optional checks fail, the output is displayed in the check, but the pull request is not blocked. This ensures that the data in the repository remains consistent over the long term and that non-urgent inconsistencies are corrected over time. Automations, Reports and Other Integrations At this point, we had achieved several important results: We designed a new data structure tailored to the workflows of the Detection Engineering team. We reorganized the existing data into this new structure. We migrated additional information scattered across manually updated Excel files and reports into the repository. We removed existing inconsistencies in the data and technically ensured that no new inconsistencies are introduced during the development process. This allowed us to establish the Git repository as the single source of truth for all detection-related data. The validator also ensures consistency across all files in the repository – for example, between the metadata documents and the corresponding technical implementations. As a result, the metadata documents can be used reliably for analysis and reporting, as they consistently reflect the deployed state in the production platforms. In Part 2 of this series, we already mentioned the CLI tool used to generate the existing Excel reports from the repository. With the achieved data quality in the repository, these reports are now far more reliable than the previously manually updated versions, which partially contained outdated data and errors introduced through human error. Furthermore, these reports can be generated automatically in pipelines and provided to other departments, such as Compliance, on a regular basis without manual effort from the Detection Engineering team. Another analysis tool uses the repository data and the DeTTECT framework to create layer files for the MITRE ATT&CK Navigator. These files provide a visual overview of detection coverage and can support the Threat Intelligence team in comparing current coverage with the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) profiles of potential attacker groups. Furthermore, we initiated a larger project: a full rework of reporting on the detection library by synchronising detection metadata into their ServiceNow ITSM (IT service management) solution. The goal is to fully remove manual reporting work, even though it is already partially automated. Non-developer stakeholders, such as management, internal audit, and external auditors, should not be expected to work with plain YAML files or navigate GitHub repositories. However, these stakeholders have a valid interest in the detection library, as they may need to ensure coverage of specific techniques for compliance reasons, oversee the development backlog, or evaluate Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). As ServiceNow is already established as a central location for different types of data, it is well suited to provide information about the detection library and make the latest data available to these non-developer stakeholders. This removes the requirement to manually update Excel files for audit purposes. ServiceNow can provide a complete view that answers questions such as: “Which detections exist for MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003.001, which are currently in development, which are planned, and which existed in the past?” In addition, ServiceNow maintains a trusted change log of values to further fulfil compliance requirements. ServiceNow will contain only information from the metadata documents, not implementation contents. No detection data can be edited from ServiceNow; GitHub remains the single source of truth. The data is collected from the repository and pushed to ServiceNow by pipelines. In addition to data for active detections from the metadata files, information displayed in ServiceNow is also taken from issues on the GitHub Project board and metadata files in the detections_retired folder. With the availability of the detection library data in ServiceNow, there is the possibility to move more related processes into ServiceNow workflows that are currently are integrated into GitHub directly. These processes could include coverage analysis (comparing the current library with threat actor profiles) as well as requesting the development of new detections. Such a ServiceNow workflow could open a new issue in GitHub on the project board. This would further reduce the number of people, who are not detection developers, that require access to the GitHub repository. Future Possibilities After these modifications to the data storage and development processes have been implemented and are running smoothly, there are further improvement opportunities to evaluate. Auto-Deployment of Detections to Test Environments With detections now organised as modular, encapsulated entities rather than scattered across files and repositories, it becomes possible to automatically create test bundles. It would be possible to fully automate the deployment of detections to a test environment. When the ticket for an ongoing development is moved to the testing status in the GitHub Project board, the modified detection in the linked pull request could be deployed to a test environment. As soon as the issue progresses further, for example to the review or completed status, the detection could be removed from the test environment again. This would ensure that every detection is tested in the exact form in which it will later be deployed because the production deployment logic would also be used in test environments. It would also remove manual steps that could introduce human error. Autonomous Test Execution In the current process, every detection must be tested before release. The detection is deployed to a test environment, its Atomic Red Team test definition is executed on a client machine in that environment, and the resulting alert is recorded in the review documentation. Currently, all these steps are performed manually. Building on the deployment automation described in the previous section, test execution and result gathering could also be automated. Following the restructuring, Atomic Red Team test definitions are organised per detection and can therefore be copied to the appropriate test machine and executed from a CI pipeline. A regularly executed job could then collect alerts generated in the test environments and match them to the corresponding test executions. Both test execution and alert collection could be reported through separate GitHub checks in the relevant pull requests, alongside the existing validator output. These CI pipeline steps could be linked to the status of an issue on the GitHub Project board, ensuring that tests run only when a detection is ready for testing and thereby keeping noise in the test environment low. This would remove repetitive manual tasks for detection engineers and reduce the risk of errors, such as executing an outdated test version. It would also remove several operational hurdles, including the need for every detection developer to have interactive access to the test machines and a limited number of concurrent RDP sessions. With this automation in place, a developer would simply move an issue to the testing status after implementing a detection and its test. The CI pipelines would then perform validation and testing, and provide the reviewer with all relevant success or failure details. This setup would also enable regular testing of the complete detection library. Without automation, existing detections can only be tested on a sample basis. With automation, the full library could be tested more frequently, allowing broken detections, for example because of missing log sources, to be identified and scheduled for rework. Generation of Splunk Configurations In the new setup, redundant information is still stored in different files. One possible next step would be to remove this redundancy by storing only the parts of a Splunk search that cannot be derived elsewhere, mainly SPL and drill-down searches. Other information could be taken from the metadata documents, such as title, severity, description, and tags, or from general configurations, such as the schedule. Transforms for simple false-positive lookups could also be generated from the filename and the CSV header in the lookup file. This would further reduce manual work, free resources, and lower the risk of errors. However, it requires auto-deployment to test environments, as there would no longer be a complete Splunk configuration in the repository that could be copied easily to a test environment. Wrapping Up Together with the customer, we streamlined the Detection Engineering process, ensured data consistency, and implemented initial reporting and automations based on the new data foundation. We also supported the definition and initiation of larger efforts that build on this foundation. All tooling implementations were built to be as modular as possible, allowing reuse and making it easier to integrate additional automations into the setup in the future.

This is not inherently problematic; the data had been structured this way for a long time. However, it creates issues when the different files contain inconsistent values. If the metadata file states a different severity from that in the actual implementation, analyses and reports based on the metadata files are incorrect. Therefore, such inconsistencies needed to be identified and corrected, and we needed to ensure that no new inconsistencies would be introduced into the repository.

To accomplish this, a validator was implemented. This validator contains numerous test cases that check files against defined requirements. These checks cover different questions:

  • Whether files are parseable, preventing malformed files from breaking other scripts and automations.
  • Whether files fulfil the defined schema, identifying missing, misspelled, or surplus keys.
  • Whether values stored in multiple files are consistent.

The checks are divided into different levels:

  • required: These checks must always pass.
  • required_on_change: These checks must pass when a detection is modified; for existing, unchanged detections, they are considered optional.
  • optional: These checks create remarks for the developer but do not block a change.

The differentiation between these levels makes the initial improvement of consistency manageable. While some issues need to be fixed before the data can be relied upon, such as severity values, MITRE ATT&CK IDs, and platforms, other data should be consistent long-term but would require too much effort to correct in a single step. Their inconsistency does not cause immediate problems, for example where Atomic Red Team test cases do not match a naming schema. These non-urgent checks become mandatory once a developer modifies the affected detection; until then, they remain optional.

Furthermore, there are scenarios in which fields that are usually identical differ for legitimate reasons. For example, some descriptions contain variables in the implementation that are populated in the Splunk UI, while the description in the metadata document remains generic.

The validator is built as a library that is used in two ways.

Firstly, it is available as a CLI tool. This tool has parameters that define which levels of checks to report. With this tool, we identified inconsistencies and corrected them manually. This sometimes required research in old tickets to determine which of two values for a field was correct, as an error could have been introduced either when defining the metadata file or when implementing the detection.

Secondly, validation is integrated into the development process through CI pipelines. When a pull request is opened, the CI pipeline runs the validation checks on the detection folders included in the pull request changeset. The result and detailed output are displayed in a GitHub check in the pull request to provide direct feedback to the detection developer. If any required or required_on_change checks fail, the pull request is automatically blocked from merging. When optional checks fail, the output is displayed in the check, but the pull request is not blocked. This ensures that the data in the repository remains consistent over the long term and that non-urgent inconsistencies are corrected over time.

Automations, Reports and Other Integrations

At this point, we had achieved several important results:

  • We designed a new data structure tailored to the workflows of the Detection Engineering team.
  • We reorganized the existing data into this new structure.
  • We migrated additional information scattered across manually updated Excel files and reports into the repository.
  • We removed existing inconsistencies in the data and technically ensured that no new inconsistencies are introduced during the development process.

This allowed us to establish the Git repository as the single source of truth for all detection-related data. The validator also ensures consistency across all files in the repository – for example, between the metadata documents and the corresponding technical implementations. As a result, the metadata documents can be used reliably for analysis and reporting, as they consistently reflect the deployed state in the production platforms.

In Part 2 of this series, we already mentioned the CLI tool used to generate the existing Excel reports from the repository. With the achieved data quality in the repository, these reports are now far more reliable than the previously manually updated versions, which partially contained outdated data and errors introduced through human error. Furthermore, these reports can be generated automatically in pipelines and provided to other departments, such as Compliance, on a regular basis without manual effort from the Detection Engineering team.

Another analysis tool uses the repository data and the DeTTECT framework to create layer files for the MITRE ATT&CK Navigator. These files provide a visual overview of detection coverage and can support the Threat Intelligence team in comparing current coverage with the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) profiles of potential attacker groups.

Furthermore, we initiated a larger project: a full rework of reporting on the detection library by synchronising detection metadata into their ServiceNow ITSM (IT service management) solution. The goal is to fully remove manual reporting work, even though it is already partially automated.

Non-developer stakeholders, such as management, internal audit, and external auditors, should not be expected to work with plain YAML files or navigate GitHub repositories. However, these stakeholders have a valid interest in the detection library, as they may need to ensure coverage of specific techniques for compliance reasons, oversee the development backlog, or evaluate Key Performance Indicators (KPIs).

As ServiceNow is already established as a central location for different types of data, it is well suited to provide information about the detection library and make the latest data available to these non-developer stakeholders. This removes the requirement to manually update Excel files for audit purposes. ServiceNow can provide a complete view that answers questions such as: “Which detections exist for MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003.001, which are currently in development, which are planned, and which existed in the past?” In addition, ServiceNow maintains a trusted change log of values to further fulfil compliance requirements.

ServiceNow will contain only information from the metadata documents, not implementation contents. No detection data can be edited from ServiceNow; GitHub remains the single source of truth. The data is collected from the repository and pushed to ServiceNow by pipelines. In addition to data for active detections from the metadata files, information displayed in ServiceNow is also taken from issues on the GitHub Project board and metadata files in the detections_retired folder.

With the availability of the detection library data in ServiceNow, there is the possibility to move more related processes into ServiceNow workflows that are currently are integrated into GitHub directly. These processes could include coverage analysis (comparing the current library with threat actor profiles) as well as requesting the development of new detections. Such a ServiceNow workflow could open a new issue in GitHub on the project board. This would further reduce the number of people, who are not detection developers, that require access to the GitHub repository.

Future Possibilities

After these modifications to the data storage and development processes have been implemented and are running smoothly, there are further improvement opportunities to evaluate.

Auto-Deployment of Detections to Test Environments

With detections now organised as modular, encapsulated entities rather than scattered across files and repositories, it becomes possible to automatically create test bundles. It would be possible to fully automate the deployment of detections to a test environment. When the ticket for an ongoing development is moved to the testing status in the GitHub Project board, the modified detection in the linked pull request could be deployed to a test environment. As soon as the issue progresses further, for example to the review or completed status, the detection could be removed from the test environment again. This would ensure that every detection is tested in the exact form in which it will later be deployed because the production deployment logic would also be used in test environments. It would also remove manual steps that could introduce human error.

Autonomous Test Execution

In the current process, every detection must be tested before release. The detection is deployed to a test environment, its Atomic Red Team test definition is executed on a client machine in that environment, and the resulting alert is recorded in the review documentation. Currently, all these steps are performed manually.

Building on the deployment automation described in the previous section, test execution and result gathering could also be automated. Following the restructuring, Atomic Red Team test definitions are organised per detection and can therefore be copied to the appropriate test machine and executed from a CI pipeline. A regularly executed job could then collect alerts generated in the test environments and match them to the corresponding test executions. Both test execution and alert collection could be reported through separate GitHub checks in the relevant pull requests, alongside the existing validator output.

These CI pipeline steps could be linked to the status of an issue on the GitHub Project board, ensuring that tests run only when a detection is ready for testing and thereby keeping noise in the test environment low.

This would remove repetitive manual tasks for detection engineers and reduce the risk of errors, such as executing an outdated test version. It would also remove several operational hurdles, including the need for every detection developer to have interactive access to the test machines and a limited number of concurrent RDP sessions.

With this automation in place, a developer would simply move an issue to the testing status after implementing a detection and its test. The CI pipelines would then perform validation and testing, and provide the reviewer with all relevant success or failure details.

This setup would also enable regular testing of the complete detection library. Without automation, existing detections can only be tested on a sample basis. With automation, the full library could be tested more frequently, allowing broken detections, for example because of missing log sources, to be identified and scheduled for rework.

Generation of Splunk Configurations

In the new setup, redundant information is still stored in different files. One possible next step would be to remove this redundancy by storing only the parts of a Splunk search that cannot be derived elsewhere, mainly SPL and drill-down searches. Other information could be taken from the metadata documents, such as title, severity, description, and tags, or from general configurations, such as the schedule. Transforms for simple false-positive lookups could also be generated from the filename and the CSV header in the lookup file.

This would further reduce manual work, free resources, and lower the risk of errors. However, it requires auto-deployment to test environments, as there would no longer be a complete Splunk configuration in the repository that could be copied easily to a test environment.

Wrapping Up

Together with the customer, we streamlined the Detection Engineering process, ensured data consistency, and implemented initial reporting and automations based on the new data foundation. We also supported the definition and initiation of larger efforts that build on this foundation. All tooling implementations were built to be as modular as possible, allowing reuse and making it easier to integrate additional automations into the setup in the future.

items.title: AI Didn’t Create a New Kind of Risk. It Removed the Time You Had to Fix the Old One.
